TERRITORIAL REACH OF CALIFORNIA WAGE AND HOUR LAW FOR INTERSTATE WORK (LAB. CODE §§ 204, 226, 510, 1171.5; SULLIVAN V. ORACLE CORP.; WARD V. UNITED AIRLINES, INC.; OMAN V. DELTA AIR LINES, INC.) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the geographic reach of California wage and hour statutes when an employee’s work is not confined to California — the situation presented by a position such as Regional Field Engineer, held by Jordan Lee and based at Oakland, California.

It describes the overtime statute’s text (Labor Code section 510); the preamble to the wage law (Labor Code section 1171.5); the California Supreme Court’s decision in Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. (2011) 51 Cal.4th 1191, holding that the overtime laws reach full days and weeks of work performed in California by nonresidents of a California-based employer, and that the unfair competition law does not reach out-of-state Fair Labor Standards Act violations; the governmental-interest conflict-of-laws analysis those courts apply; the companion decisions in Ward v. United Airlines, Inc. (2020) 9 Cal.5th 732 and Oman v. Delta Air Lines, Inc. (2020) 9 Cal.5th 762, which tie Labor Code sections 226 and 204 to the employee’s principal place of work and, for interstate transportation workers, to the employee’s base of work operations; and the questions the courts expressly left open.

This sheet describes what the authorities say. It does not determine which state’s law governs any particular employee, does not classify any position, and does not predict how any court would resolve a dispute.

THE OVERTIME STATUTE SPEAKS TO WORK, NOT TO WORKERS’ RESIDENCE
California’s daily and weekly overtime requirement is stated in Labor Code section 510, subdivision (a). The subdivision opens by declaring that eight hours of labor constitutes a day’s work, and then fixes premium rates by reference to the work performed: any work beyond eight hours in a workday, any work beyond 40 hours in a workweek, and the first eight hours on the seventh day of work in a workweek draw one and one-half times the regular rate; work beyond 12 hours in a day, and work beyond eight hours on a seventh day, draw twice the regular rate. The subdivision then lists three categories of alternative workweek schedules to which the section’s requirements do not apply (sections 511, 514, and 554).

Nothing in the operative language conditions the obligation on where the employee lives, where the employer is incorporated or headquartered, or where the employee works at other times. The measuring units the statute uses are the workday and the workweek.

SULLIVAN V. ORACLE CORP.: OVERTIME LAW REACHES FULL DAYS AND WEEKS WORKED HERE BY NONRESIDENTS
In Sullivan v. Oracle Corp., the California Supreme Court answered questions certified by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit about nonresident instructors who worked mainly in Colorado and Arizona but also spent whole days working in California for a California-headquartered employer. The court began with the statutory text and read it as speaking to employment in the state rather than to the employee’s residence, observing that the Legislature knows how to write an exception for nonresidents and has not written one into the overtime law, though it has authorized exemptions on a variety of other bases.

The court answered the first certified question by holding that the Labor Code’s overtime provisions applied to the plaintiffs’ work performed in California. The plaintiffs in that case claimed overtime only for entire days and weeks worked in California, matching the units the overtime statute itself uses.

THE PREAMBLE TO THE WAGE LAW: PROTECTIONS AVAILABLE TO ALL INDIVIDUALS EMPLOYED IN THIS STATE
Labor Code section 1171.5 is a set of legislative findings placed at the head of the chapter of the Labor Code governing wages, hours, and working conditions. Subdivision (a) declares that all protections, rights, and remedies available under state law, with an exception for a reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law, are available to all individuals regardless of immigration status who have applied for employment, or who are or have been employed, in this state.

Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. treated this subdivision as confirming that the wage law speaks to all individuals employed in the state, and rejected the argument that the provision reaches only undocumented workers. Ward v. United Airlines, Inc. later read the same provision from the opposite direction: the employee there argued that California residence should itself bring an employee within section 226, and the court answered that the provision weighs against making residence the decisive factor just as it weighs against treating nonresidence as disqualifying.

TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION AND THE TIDEWATER CAUTION AGAINST BROAD EXTRATERRITORIAL READINGS
Government Code section 110 states that the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the State extends to all places within its boundaries as established by the constitution. Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. cited that section alongside the court’s earlier decision in Tidewater Marine Western, Inc. v. Bradshaw (1996) 14 Cal.4th 557, which held that Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders reached crew members working on boats inside California’s state-law boundaries in the Santa Barbara Channel. As Sullivan reproduces it, Tidewater said that California employment laws implicitly extend to employment occurring within the state’s state-law boundaries.

Sullivan also read Tidewater as having deliberately declined to settle the outer limits in either direction: Tidewater was not prepared to hold that the wage orders apply to all employment in California and never to employment outside California. Sullivan described that reservation as foreseeing only a limited and reciprocal extraterritorial possibility, and said nothing in Tidewater supports allowing a nonresident to work entire days or weeks in California outside the protection of California law.

THE CONFLICT-OF-LAWS STEP: GOVERNMENTAL INTEREST ANALYSIS
Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. treated the geographic question as having two parts: first, whether the California statute by its terms reaches the work, and second, which state’s law governs if another state also purports to regulate the same work. For the second part the court applied governmental interest analysis, the method California courts have used for decades, which proceeds in three steps — whether the potentially affected states’ laws differ; if so, whether each state has an interest in applying its own law such that a true conflict exists; and, if there is a true conflict, which state’s interest would be more impaired if its policy were subordinated.

Applying those steps, the court found the existence of a true conflict doubtful at best, because Arizona had no overtime law and Colorado’s own regulation reached only work performed within Colorado. Assuming a conflict for argument’s sake, the court concluded that subordinating California’s interests would bring about the greater impairment, because nonresidents working here without overtime protection would lose the statute’s health-and-safety and anti-overwork purposes entirely.

THE ANALYSIS IS MADE STATUTE BY STATUTE, NOT ONCE FOR ALL OF WAGE LAW
Both Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. and the 2020 companion decisions state that a conclusion about one California labor protection does not carry over to the others. Sullivan said the case presented no issue about any provision of California wage law other than overtime, and contrasted the state’s strong interest in overtime compensation for work performed here with its interest in matters such as the contents of an out-of-state business’s pay stubs or the treatment of vacation time, which the court said may or may not be sufficient to displace another state’s law.

Ward v. United Airlines, Inc. repeated the point in a footnote, saying that what it held was specific to Labor Code section 226 and would not necessarily apply to the state’s minimum wage, equal pay, or antiharassment laws. Oman v. Delta Air Lines, Inc. said the same thing in the body of its opinion, adding that the rules articulated for sections 204 and 226 do not resolve whether the minimum wage laws apply.

THE PRESUMPTION AGAINST EXTRATERRITORIALITY AND THE UNFAIR COMPETITION LAW
The third question answered in Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. was whether the plaintiffs could use their employer’s alleged federal Fair Labor Standards Act violations, committed in other states, as the predicate unlawful acts for a claim under California’s unfair competition law. The court held they could not.

The court framed the issue through the presumption against extraterritorial application: absent a clearly expressed or reasonably inferable legislative intention, a California statute is not treated as operative with respect to occurrences outside the state. Finding nothing in the unfair competition law’s language or history to displace that presumption, the court held that the presumption applies to that statute in full force, and went on to conclude that borrowing out-of-state Fair Labor Standards Act violations would make the statute operate impermissibly as to occurrences outside California.

WARD V. UNITED AIRLINES: TERRITORIAL PRESUMPTIONS ALONE DO NOT DECIDE INTERSTATE CASES
Ward v. United Airlines, Inc. arose from wage statement claims by California-resident pilots and flight attendants of an airline incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Illinois; the crew members performed most of their work outside California’s jurisdiction. Labor Code section 226, subdivision (a), requires an employer, semimonthly or at each payment of wages, to furnish an accurate itemized written statement showing nine enumerated categories of information, and the crew members alleged the airline’s statements omitted some of them.

The court identified two competing interpretive presumptions — one against extraterritorial application of state law and a mirror-image presumption in favor of applying state law to conduct within the state — and said neither could resolve the case, because from any given state’s perspective an interstate employee’s claims may have both extraterritorial and intraterritorial elements.

WARD’S TEST: PRINCIPAL PLACE OF WORK, AND FOR INTERSTATE TRANSPORTATION WORKERS, BASE OF OPERATIONS
Ward v. United Airlines, Inc. concluded that entitlement to California-compliant wage statements turns on whether the employee’s principal place of work is in California. That is satisfied when the employee spends the majority of working hours in California. For employees whose work is not predominantly performed in any one state, the court inferred that the Legislature intended section 226 to apply where California is the state with the most significant relationship to the work, and it supplied a second, sequential inquiry: the employee performs some work in California and is based in California, meaning California is the physical location where the worker presents himself or herself to begin work.

The court drew that structure from the unemployment insurance coverage rules the Legislature adopted for employees whose work is not localized in any one state (Unemployment Insurance Code sections 602 and 603), and stated its conclusion in the same two-part form when it answered the certified question.

Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the geographic reach of California wage and hour statutes when an employee’s work is not confined to California — the situation presented by a position such as Regional Field Engineer, held by Jordan Lee and based at Oakland, California.

It describes the overtime statute’s text (Labor Code section 510); the preamble to the wage law (Labor Code section 1171.5); the California Supreme Court’s decision in Sullivan v. Oracle Corp. (2011) 51 Cal.4th 1191, holding that the overtime laws reach full days and weeks of work performed in California by nonresidents of a California-based employer, and that the unfair competition law does not reach out-of-state Fair Labor Standards Act violations; the governmental-interest conflict-of-laws analysis those courts apply; the companion decisions in Ward v. (2020) 9 Cal.5th 762, which tie Labor Code sections 226 and 204 to the employee’s principal place of work and, for interstate transportation workers, to the employee’s base of work operations; and the questions the courts expressly left open.

This sheet describes what the authorities say. It does not determine which state’s law governs any particular employee, does not classify any position, and does not predict how any court would resolve a dispute.

California’s daily and weekly overtime requirement is stated in Labor Code section 510, subdivision (a). The subdivision opens by declaring that eight hours of labor constitutes a day’s work, and then fixes premium rates by reference to the work performed: any work beyond eight hours in a workday, any work beyond 40 hours in a workweek, and the first eight hours on the seventh day of work in a workweek draw one and one-half times the regular rate; work beyond 12 hours in a day, and work beyond eight hours on a seventh day, draw twice the regular rate. Nothing in the operative language conditions the obligation on where the employee lives, where the employer is incorporated or headquartered, or where the employee works at other times. The measuring units the statute uses are the workday and the workweek.

Oracle Corp. treated the geographic question as having two parts: first, whether the California statute by its terms reaches the work, and second, which state’s law governs if another state also purports to regulate the same work. For the second part the court applied governmental interest analysis, the method California courts have used for decades, which proceeds in three steps — whether the potentially affected states’ laws differ; if so, whether each state has an interest in applying its own law such that a true conflict exists; and, if there is a true conflict, which state’s interest would be more impaired if its policy were subordinated.
